stem: Three weeks after solid-organ transplantation, a recipient develops symptoms consistent with human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) reactivation. Which timing description aligns with standard post-transplant infection references?

options.text: Onset typically occurs between 2 and 4 weeks posttransplantation
HHV-6 reactivation occurs only before the transplant operation
HHV-6 disease is expected exclusively after 12 months
HHV-6 never occurs with CMV coinfection

explanation.rationale_correct: HHV-6 is usually reactivation of endogenous latent virus with onset typically between 2 and 4 weeks posttransplantation; CMV coinfection is common.

rationale_incorrect.B: HHV-6 is described as post-transplant reactivation rather than a preoperative-only event.
rationale_incorrect.C: Standard references place typical HHV-6 onset in the early post-transplant period rather than after 12 months.
rationale_incorrect.D: CMV coinfection with HHV-6 is described as common.

stem: Six weeks after transplantation on higher maintenance immunosuppression, a recipient develops adenovirus infection. Which epidemiologic pattern aligns with standard references?

options.text: Adenovirus is most common in the first 3 months after transplant and with higher immunosuppression dosing
Adenovirus occurs only more than 2 years after every transplant
Adenovirus risk decreases when immunosuppression dosing is higher
Adenovirus is limited to conjunctival infection without other organ involvement

explanation.rationale_correct: Adenovirus may cause respiratory, GI, conjunctival, or disseminated pathology and is most common in the first 3 months after transplant with higher immunosuppression dosing.

rationale_incorrect.B: References emphasize early post-transplant timing rather than exclusive late disease after 2 years.
rationale_incorrect.C: Higher immunosuppression dosing is associated with greater adenovirus risk rather than lower risk.
rationale_incorrect.D: Adenovirus may involve respiratory, GI, conjunctival, or disseminated pathology rather than conjunctiva alone.

stem: A pediatric kidney transplant recipient is evaluated for possible acute rejection. Which presentation aligns with standard pediatric kidney references?

options.text: Hypertension, pain over the graft area, and hematuria
Isolated slapped-cheek rash without laboratory changes
Expected absence of any blood-pressure or urine changes during rejection
Rejection limited to adult recipients with no pediatric manifestations

explanation.rationale_correct: Children with kidney rejection may present with decreased urine output, increased weight, hypertension, increased creatinine, pain over the graft area, and other signs such as proteinuria or hematuria.

rationale_incorrect.B: Slapped-cheek rash suggests infections such as parvovirus rather than typical rejection presentation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Pediatric rejection commonly includes hypertension, creatinine changes, and urinary abnormalities.
rationale_incorrect.D: Pediatric kidney recipients have described rejection presentations distinct from assuming rejection does not occur in children.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 17, Pediatric Kidney Transplantation → rejection → i.

stem: An adult kidney transplant recipient has delayed graft function without primary nonfunction. Which early postoperative management approach aligns with standard complication references?

options.text: Supportive therapies such as dialysis until graft function improves
Immediate relisting for retransplantation in every case on postoperative day 1
Permanent discontinuation of all immunosuppression until creatinine normalizes
No supportive care is available while awaiting graft recovery

explanation.rationale_correct: Delayed graft function may require supportive therapies to maintain optimal patient status until graft function improves; dialysis is among organ-specific supportive options.

rationale_incorrect.B: Primary graft nonfunction may prompt relisting, but delayed graft function is managed supportively while function may recover.
rationale_incorrect.C: Immunosuppression is continued per protocol rather than stopped entirely during delayed graft function.
rationale_incorrect.D: Supportive therapies including dialysis are available during delayed graft function.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → postoperative complications → ii. Delayed graft function
